papers.title: Projecting Introduction Timelines for Cholera Conjugate Vaccine and Typhoid-Cholera Conjugate Combo Vaccine: A Scenario-Based Forecasting Approach
papers.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to project introduction timing and pathways of cholera conjugate vaccine (CCV) and combined typhoid-cholera conjugate vaccines (TCV/CCVs) in 39 low- and middle-income countries and to assess potential barriers to their routine immunization integration. Methods: Accelerated failure time models were fitted using oral cholera vaccine (OCV) introduction as a proxy for CCV adoption. Country-level estimates were standardized using observed post-WHO-prequalification introduction intervals for analogous vaccine transitions. TCV/CCV introduction timing and pathways were projected by combining standardized CCV estimates with a TCV introduction priority index based on typhoid burden and previous vaccination experience. Potential barriers to routine immunization integration were assessed using semi-quantitative scoring approach. Results: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) eligibility, greater previous OCV experience, and higher cholera intensity were associated with earlier introduction times. After standardization, the median projected time to CCV introduction was 6.9 years after WHO prequalification, with 12 countries introducing within five years. The TCV/CCV projections comprised three pathways: CCV introduction followed by transition to TCV/CCV, direct TCV/CCV introduction and continued CCV use without TCV/CCV introduction during the analysis period. Projected introduction timing was not consistently aligned with routine integration barrier levels for either vaccine. Conclusions: These scenario-based projections provide an early indication of where and when demand may emerge and which countries may require additional programmatic or financing support. The findings can inform demand forecasting, market assessment, manufacturing and supply planning, investment decisions, and introduction preparedness, but the projections should be recalibrated as product-specific evidence becomes available.

papers.title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study
papers.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. Objective To compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three cliniciansone each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. Results The GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (-0.22, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. Conclusions Our findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents in Sekondi-Takoradi, Western Region of Ghana: A community-based cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Mpox re-emerged as a global public health concern in 2022, and the Western Region of Ghana became the epicentre of the countrys largest recorded outbreak in 2025. Ahead of a sub-national vaccination campaign launched in October 2025, no study had examined the determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents of the region using a theoretically grounded framework. This study determined the sociodemographic and Health Belief Model-based determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents of the Sekondi-Takoradi Metropolis, Western Region, Ghana. A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 580 adults in six purposively selected peri-urban areas and their surrounding communities between July and August 2025, before the vaccination campaign began. Vaccine acceptance was measured as a three-category outcome (accept, hesitant, refuse) and analysed using chi square tests and multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, Health Belief Model constructs, and peri-urban area. Overall, 75.7% of respondents were willing to accept the vaccine, 12.9% were hesitant and 11.4% would refuse. Perceived vaccine safety was the strongest determinant: respondents who considered the vaccine very safe had markedly lower adjusted odds of hesitancy (adjusted odds ratio 0.02, 95% confidence interval 0.00-0.12) and refusal (0.03, 0.01-0.13) than those who considered it unsafe. Uncertainty about vaccine effectiveness was associated with hesitancy (9.83, 1.95-49.50), and belief in its effectiveness with lower odds of refusal (0.22, 0.06-0.86). Higher educational attainment was associated with lower odds of hesitancy, being a student or employed with lower odds of refusal, and acceptance differed be 1 tween peri-urban areas (55.1% to 95.6%). Knowledge of mpox transmission was associated with acceptance in bivariate analysis (p < 0.001) but not after adjustment. Risk communication that addresses vaccine safety and effectiveness, rather than generic disease-awareness messaging alone, is likely to be most effec tive in improving mpox vaccine acceptance in this population, with unemployed and less-educated residents warranting targeting. As a pre-campaign baseline collected during an active outbreak, these findings can inform the vaccination response in the Western Region and preparedness in comparable peri-urban West African settings.

papers.title: Determinants of early child development among children aged 24-59 months in Ethiopia: 2024-25 Demographic and Health Survey
papers.abstract: Background: The 2024-25 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS) is Ethiopia's first national survey to measure early childhood development using UNICEF's Early Childhood Development Index 2030 (ECDI2030). This provides a national estimate for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 4.2.1, the proportion of children aged 24-59 months who are developmentally on track. We estimated the prevalence of being developmentally on track and examined its child, maternal, household and community determinants in Ethiopia. Methods: This cross-sectional study analysed 3,731 children aged 24-59 months (weighted n = 3,514) of 3,232 mothers in 771 clusters. Children were on track if they achieved the age-specific minimum number of the 20 ECDI2030 milestones. Prevalence was estimated with design-based methods. Four three-level mixed-effects logistic regression models (children within mothers within clusters) were fitted, and interviewer effects were assessed. Results: Overall, 36.3% (95% CI 33.4-39.3) of children were developmentally on track. Prevalence ranged from 23.3% in Southwest Regional State, Ethiopia, to 77.7% in Addis Ababa. In the null model, 21.5% of the variation lay between clusters (median odds ratio 3.24). In the final model, the odds of being on track were lower at 36-47 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 0.57, 95% CI 0.44-0.74) and 48-59 months (AOR 0.39, 0.30-0.51) than at 24-35 months. They were also lower after a preceding birth interval under 24 months (AOR 0.75, 0.57-0.99), after recent diarrhoea, fever or cough (AOR 0.59, 0.45-0.77), and where distance to a health facility was a big problem (AOR 0.61, 0.48-0.79). Odds were higher for girls (AOR 1.38, 1.12-1.70), with maternal education (more than secondary vs none: AOR 2.08, 1.19-3.63) and with weekly media exposure (AOR 2.15, 1.51-3.06). The covariates explained 55.9% of the between-cluster variance. Conclusions: Nearly two in three Ethiopian children aged 24-59 months are not developmentally on track, and children fall further behind as they age. Interventions should target maternal education, access to information and health services, birth spacing and childhood illness, with priority for the lowest-performing regions and communities.

papers.title: Gender Differences in Socioeconomic Inequalities in Body Mass Index and Health-Related Mediators Among Young and Early Midlife Finns
papers.abstract: Introduction: Socioeconomic differences in body mass index (BMI) are well established, but less is known about gender differences and their behavioral pathways. We examined gender differences in the association between socioeconomic position (SEP) and BMI, and whether dietary factors and physical activity mediated the associations. Methods: We used survey data from the employees of the City of Helsinki aged 19-39 collected in 2017 (n = 4,400, 80% women). SEP was measured by highest educational attainment, and the examined mediators were consumption of fruit and vegetables, red and processed meat, sweets and confectionery and alcohol as well as leisure-time vigorous physical activity (VPA) and sedentary time. We conducted gender-specific multiple mediation analyses using structural equation modeling and additional analyses using multiple imputation by chained equations. Results: With increasing educational attainment, mean BMI decreased from 26.4 kg/m2 to 24.0 kg/m2 among women, and from 26.6 kg/m2 to 25.2 kg/m2 among men. Lower SEP was associated with lower consumption of fruit and vegetables, higher consumption of red and processed meat, and lower VPA in both genders. Women reported healthier diets but less VPA than men. The strongest SEP-BMI mediator among women was VPA (indirect effect: 0.35, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.26, 0.44), followed by fruit and vegetable consumption (0.15, 95% CI 0.08, 0.23) and red and processed meat consumption (0.06, 95% CI 0.02, 0.11). Among men, significant mediators were red and processed meat consumption (0.12, 95% CI 0.03, 0.23), sedentary time (0.11, 95% CI 0.01, 0.24) and VPA (0.10, 95% CI 0.02, 0.21). Conclusions: Socioeconomic inequalities in BMI appear stronger among women and are shaped through partly different mechanisms between genders. Improving VPA may be relevant among low-SEP women, whereas reducing sedentary time may be more relevant among low-SEP men. Reducing red and processed meat is beneficial for both genders.

papers.title: Functional difficulty among children and adolescents aged 5-17 years in Ethiopia: Multilevel analysis of the nationally representative 2024-2025 DHS
papers.abstract: Background: Population-based data on functional difficulty among school-age children in Ethiopia are scarce. The 2024-2025 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS) included, for the first time, the UNICEF/Washington Group Child Functioning Module (CFM) for children aged 5-17 years. We estimated the prevalence and domain distribution of functional difficulty and associated factors in Ethiopia. Methods: We analysed cross-sectional EDHS data from 11,122 children aged 5-17 years (weighted n = 10,726) and 4,739 mothers. Functional difficulty was defined as "a lot of difficulty" or "cannot do at all" in any of 11 domains, or daily anxiety or depression. We estimated design-based prevalence and fitted multilevel logistic regression models (children within mothers within clusters) for any, non-affective and affective difficulty. Interviewer effects were examined with random-intercept models and within-cluster comparisons. Results: Overall, 9.5% (95% CI 8.1-11.1) of children had functional difficulty. Daily depression (6.8%) and anxiety (6.6%) dominated, and 70.3% of affected children had only affective difficulty. Difficulty in at least one non-affective domain affected 2.8% (2.2-3.7), with each domain at 0.5-1.4%. Prevalence ranged from 1.5% in Southwest Regional State, Ethiopia, to 16.5% in Oromia Regional State. In adjusted models, children not attending school had higher odds of non-affective difficulty (AOR 2.82, 95% CI 2.01-3.96), and girls had lower odds (AOR 0.63, 0.48-0.84). Outcomes clustered strongly within families (sibling correlation 67.7%) and clusters (ICC 20.9%). Six of 163 interviewers (7.9% of the weighted sample) contributed 58.2% of weighted cases of daily anxiety or depression; in the same clusters they recorded daily symptoms for 56.4% of children, against 2.1% for other interviewers. Excluding 11 statistically outlying interviewers reduced the prevalence of any difficulty to 4.6% (3.6-5.8) and of daily anxiety or depression to 3.3%. The associations with school non-attendance and sex were unchanged. Conclusions: Functional difficulties across the sensory, physical, cognitive, and affective domains, including anxiety or depression, affect about 2-3% of Ethiopian children aged 5-17 years and are strongly associated with being out of school. Appropriate interventions and resource allocation should be considered.

papers.title: The Evolving Role of Telehealth in Routine Health Care Delivery Among US Adults, 2022-2024
papers.abstract: Background: Telehealth use expanded rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, but its role following the end of the public health emergency (PHE) remains incompletely understood. This study examined changes in telehealth utilization among US adults between 2022 and 2024, characteristics associated with use, and changes in self-reported reasons for using telehealth to understand its evolving role. Methods: This serial cross-sectional study analyzed nationally representative data from 13 141 US adults participating in the Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) in 2022, during the COVID-19 PHE, and 2024, after the PHE ended. Survey-weighted analyses were used to estimate telehealth utilization and self-reported reasons for use. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was used to examine changes between survey cycles and sociodemographic and health-related characteristics associated with telehealth utilization. Multiple imputation was used to address missing data. Results: Telehealth utilization declined from 39.3% in 2022 to 34.5% in 2024; after adjustment for sociodemographic and health-related characteristics, the odds of telehealth use were significantly lower in 2024 than in 2022 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Telehealth utilization differed across population groups. Higher odds of use were observed among adults aged 35 to 49 years (aOR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.19-1.82), those with a college degree or higher (aOR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.31-2.86), those with diagnosed depression or anxiety (aOR, 2.86; 95% CI, 2.46-3.33), those with a history of cancer (aOR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.15-1.69), and insured adults (aOR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.13-2.04). All self-reported reasons for telehealth use declined between 2022 and 2024. Infection avoidance decreased from 50.2% to 19.1% and provider recommendation or requirement from 72.8% to 47.2%, whereas convenience showed a smaller decline from 65.6% to 56.2% and became the leading reported reason for telehealth use in 2024. Conclusions: Telehealth utilization declined between 2022 and 2024, while the relative persistence of convenience as a reason for use suggests a shift away from pandemic-driven demand toward more selective integration into routine health care. Differences in utilization across population groups suggest that telehealth may address some barriers to conventional care while access remains uneven. These findings highlight the evolving role of telehealth after the COVID-19 PHE and the importance of supporting its appropriate and equitable integration into routine care.

papers.title: Measuring community building in group antenatal care: Evidence from a randomized trial in Malawi
papers.abstract: Improving the quality of antenatal care is essential for reducing persistently high maternal and neonatal mortality in Malawi. Group antenatal care has demonstrated improvements in quality, satisfaction, health behaviors, and outcomes. However, the impact of community building, one of the models core components, has not previously been quantitatively assessed. This study examined the measurement properties of two community building measures, assessed the impact of group antenatal care on these measures, and explored their potential role as mediators of health outcomes. This secondary analysis used quantitative data from the parent study testing the effectiveness of group antenatal care at seven clinics in Blantyre District, Malawi. The Perinatal Peer Support Scale and the Provider Connectedness subscale of the Pregnancy Related Empowerment Scale were used to measure community building and were validated using factor analyses. Results supported a two-factor structure for perinatal peer support (relational support and peer network) and a unidimensional structure for provider connectedness. Using generalized linear modeling, we found that participation in group antenatal care was associated with significantly stronger community building across all measures when compared to usual individual antenatal care. Women in group antenatal care demonstrated higher relational support score, peer network, and provider connectedness scores compared with women in individual antenatal care (p < 0.001). However, we found no evidence that community building had direct or indirect (mediating) effects on maternal psychological distress or infant birthweight. This study strengthens the evidence base for group antenatal care by validating measures of community building and showing that relational support, peer networks, and provider connectedness are important benefits of participation. Although community building did not mediate the outcomes examined here, the findings highlight the need to further test of theoretical pathways linking group antenatal care to maternal and child health outcomes.

papers.title: Age-related Trust and its Association with Cost-related Medication Nonadherence
papers.abstract: Trust operates foundationally at the personal and societal levels, a vital force that drives social connection, cooperation, and positive outcomes. In healthcare, trust is instrumental in improving patient outcomes as it forms the foundation for shared decision-making and patient-provider relationships. With growing evidence that generalized trust toward other people grows with age and behaviors such as cost-related medication non-adherence (CRN) decrease with age we study whether lack of trust is a force that drives up CRN and its variability in effects across age groups, controlling for other risk factors. The data consists of 680 Medicare diabetes patients at high risk of hospitalization enrolled in a randomized controlled trial of the effect of the Comprehensive Care Physician model (CCP) at an academic medical center between November 2012 and June 2016. This study provides first-of-its-kind evidence that lack of trust is an important force that drives up CRN and the effect of lack of trust decreased even though the lack of trust decreased by age increments. The effect of lack of trust is particularly pronounced among younger patients. For practice and policy, it shows the potential promising prospect that a more trusting attitude may be conducive to more productive health. More research is needed on how to build trust at the societal level and in healthcare specifically, and how generalized trust and target-specific trust of providers are correlated.

papers.title: Displaced by a Volcano: Adolescent Well-Being in Uncertain Times in Iceland 2023-2026
papers.abstract: Aims: The November 2023 evacuation of Grindavik, Iceland, left families facing prolonged uncertainty about return. We examined adolescent well-being before and after evacuation and changes in gaps with national peers between 2025 and 2026. Methods: Repeated cross-sectional analyses used the 2023, 2025, and 2026 Icelandic Youth Study waves, adjusting for grade, gender, and non-Icelandic background. The town's single school in 2023 provided the pre-evacuation benchmark, with models accounting for national time trends. Adolescents who moved before evacuation provided a mobility benchmark. Results: In 2025, evacuees reported lower life satisfaction and school belonging, more psychosomatic symptoms, and higher odds of school absence and past-30-day substance use than the national reference group. The three well-being outcomes departed from the pre-evacuation pattern. Life-satisfaction and belonging gaps were larger among girls than boys in 2025, but these gender differences narrowed by 2026. Comparisons with prior movers suggested a distinct evacuation-related pattern in 2025 among evacuee girls, who reported lower life satisfaction and school belonging than prior-mover girls. In 2026, psychosomatic symptoms (B = 0.29, 95% CI [0.08, 0.49]), absenteeism (OR = 1.81, 95% CI [1.26, 2.60]), and substance use (OR = 2.59, 95% CI [1.75, 3.84]) remained higher relative to the national reference group. Life satisfaction and belonging were directionally lower, with intervals including zero. Change estimates did not establish narrowing of the gaps. Conclusions: The findings underscore the need for sustained educational and well-being support to address adolescents' social connections alongside their mental health during prolonged displacement, including in a Nordic welfare setting.

papers.title: PNEUMOCOCCAL CONJUGATE VACCINE SCHEDULES SHAPE SEROTYPE-SPECIFIC MEMORY B-CELL RESPONSES
papers.abstract: Reduced-dose pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) schedules (1+1; one primary and one booster) are now endorsed by the World Health Organisation under specific circumstances. Serotype-specific memory B cells (BMEM) are a marker of long-term protection but data from infant reduced-dose trials remain limited. As part of a randomised controlled trial in Vietnamese infants, we characterised serotype-specific BMEM responses in randomised subsets (N=50 per vaccine group per timepoint) following 0+1 (at 12 months of age) or 1+1 (2 and 12 months of age) schedules of PCV10 or PCV13, using a multimer spectral flow cytometry approach. Blood samples were collected at 12 months of age (baseline) and at day 7 and day 28 post-vaccination. A one or two dose schedule of either PCV induced robust serotype-specific BMEM responses at day 7 and day 28 for most serotypes. PCV13 generated earlier and higher BMEM responses than PCV10, while 1+1 schedules for either PCV produced higher BMEM responses than the 0+1 schedules at day 7. By day 28, these differences between the 0+1 and 1+1 schedules were no longer apparent. Notably, BMEM responses for serotypes 6B and 23F were detectable even in infants who did not achieve protective levels of serotype-specific IgG greater or equal to 0.35 ug/mL. PCV13 generated higher plasmablast and plasma cell responses by day 7, and higher cTfh responses by day 28, compared to PCV10. These findings show that 1+1 schedules of PCV10 or PCV13 induce robust BMEM responses, with important implications for the evaluation of PCVs and understanding long-term protection.

papers.title: Implementing community-based minimally invasive tissue sampling for mortality surveillance in rural South Africa: A process evaluation of the Vukamberi project
papers.abstract: Accurate cause-of-death data are limited in rural low- and middle-income settings, where most deaths occur at home without medical certification. Minimally invasive tissue sampling (MITS) is a culturally acceptable alternative to complete autopsy but has largely been applied to stillbirths and child deaths. We evaluated the process and implementation of a community-based, all-age MITS study in rural South Africa. The Vukamberi project ("to examine" in Xitsonga) is a prospective study in rural Bushbuckridge sub-district, Mpumalanga Province. Guided by the Medical Research Council Framework for Complex Interventions and Proctors Implementation Outcomes Framework, we assessed reach, adoption, fidelity, feasibility, acceptability and timeliness using prospectively collected records of deaths notified between 07 July 2024 to 30 June 2026, and mapped challenges to adaptive strategies by domain and phase. All 408 notified community deaths were screened, and 316 (77.5%) were eligible. Families consented for 206 eligible cases (65.2%), all of which proceeded to MITS, with target-organ sampling adherence in 199 (96.6%). Median time from death to notification was 15 hours (interquartile range [IQR] 5-23) and to MITS completion 37 hours (IQR 25-49). Enrolled decedents were 197 adults (95.6%) and 9 paediatric cases (4.4%). Main ineligibility reasons were in-hospital death (excluded by design; 27 cases) and notification beyond 48 hours (26 cases). Family refusal, mostly reflecting grief-related unreadiness and sociocultural barriers, accounted for 53 (48.2%) non-enrolled eligible cases. Adaptive strategies that increased enrolment included extending recruitment beyond the Agincourt Health and Socio-Demographic Surveillance System into the wider sub-district, incentivised community informants, elder-mediated consent, gender-appropriate field staff, non-disfigurement messaging in local languages and mortuary-based consenting where household access was restricted by a traditional leader. Community-based MITS was feasible in this rural setting. Culturally responsive consent strategies, mortuary partnerships and multi-channel death notification helped overcome sociocultural and logistical barriers, and a reliable supply of consumables proved essential for continuous enrolment. These findings may inform community-based mortality surveillance in other low- and middle-income settings.

papers.title: Wealth inequalities malaria parasitaemia and child anaemia in Nigeria
papers.abstract: Anaemia and malaria remain concentrated among children living in poorer households in Nigeria, but the extent to which the wealth gradient in anaemia operates through current malaria parasitaemia is uncertain. We used three nationally representative surveys to estimate a clearly defined parasitaemia-mediated component of the association, while recognising that anaemia has multiple infectious, nutritional, genetic, and social causes. We analysed de facto children aged 6-59 months in the 2010, 2015, and 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Surveys. Within each survey, we contrasted children in the poorest quintile with children in the richer and richest quintiles. The outcome was altitude-adjusted anaemia and the mediator was microscopy-confirmed parasitaemia. Weighted outcome and mediator models adjusted for child age and sex, maternal education, urban residence, geopolitical zone, household size, rainy-season interview, and altitude. We standardized interventional total, direct, and indirect effects using g-computation. Missing data were addressed with 20 chained-equation imputations; uncertainty used 1,000 Rao-Wu survey-bootstrap replicates. Analytic samples included 3,307, 3,643, and 6,572 children in 2010, 2015, and 2021. The multiple-imputation total risk difference was 11.0 (95% CI 4.1 to 17.9) percentage points in 2015 and 12.5 (95% CI 8.4 to 16.6) points in 2021; corresponding parasitaemia-mediated indirect differences were 3.4 (95% CI 1.4 to 5.4) and 2.0 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.9) points. The 2010 total-effect interval included zero. Proportion-mediated estimates were withheld for 2010 and 2015 because of unstable total-effect denominators. The poorest-to-richer/richest contrast was associated with higher anaemia risk in 2015 and 2021. A smaller positive component was compatible with mediation through microscopy-confirmed parasitaemia. Because wealth, parasitaemia, and haemoglobin were measured in the same survey visit, the estimates require assumptions about temporal ordering and unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding; they do not establish that eliminating parasitaemia would remove the observed anaemia inequality.

papers.title: Disease-Specific Trends and Ethnic Inequities in In-Hospital Cardiovascular Mortality in Suriname, 2013-2022
papers.abstract: Objective To examine temporal trends in in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalized with heart failure, ischemic heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease in Suriname from 2013 to 2022, and to assess differences according to age, sex, and ethnicity. Methods Conducted a retrospective hospital-based observational study using routinely collected discharge data from three major public hospitals in Suriname. These hospitals accounted for approximately 71.8% of national hospital admissions. Admissions with a primary diagnosis of HF (ICD-10 I50), IHD (I20-I25), or Stroke (I60-I69) were included. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for each disease, adjusting for calendar year, age, sex, and ethnicity. Results Among 84,691 admissions, 42,301 were IHD, 24,584 for Stroke, and 17,806 for HF. In-hospital mortality declined significantly across all three conditions, with adjusted odds decreasing by 14% annually for HF (aOR 0.858; 95% CI 0.841-0.875), 6% for IHD (aOR 0.941; 95% CI 0.914-0.969), and 5% for Stroke (aOR 0.947; 95% CI 0.931-0.963). Increasing age was associated with higher mortality in IHD and Stroke. Female sex was associated with lower mortality in HF (aOR 0.835; 95% CI 0.744-0.937). Ethnic disparities were most pronounced for Stroke, with higher mortality among Maroon, Creole, Javanese, and Other groups than Hindustani patients. Conclusions In-hospital mortality declined across cardiovascular conditions, but improvements were heterogeneous. Pronounced ethnic inequalities in Stroke mortality and age-related gradients highlight the need for equity-focused cardiovascular surveillance and provide a baseline for evaluating future health-system and prevention initiatives in Suriname.

papers.title: Intersectional Inequalities in Mental Health Need and Youth Justice Contact among Pupils enrolled in Alternative Provision
papers.abstract: Background. Unmet mental health and education needs increase the risk of youth justice contact. Understanding inequalities in alternative provision (AP) and how these relate to school recorded mental health needs or police criminalisation may identify opportunities to intervene. Methods. We analysed population-level linked school and police administrative data for 3.7m pupils (born 1997-2003) who attended state schools in England. We examined differences by racial-ethnic group and gender in rates and timing of AP enrolment and recording patterns of mental health-related provision and youth justice contacts among pupils with AP enrolment. Results. Our findings indicate heightened mental health need and vulnerability to criminalisation among pupils recorded with AP enrolment. Enrolment was highest among Irish Traveller and Romani pupils, followed by Black Caribbean and Mixed White-Black Caribbean pupils. Boys were enrolled more than girls, but some girls had higher rates than boys from other groups. Over 50% boys from Black Caribbean and Mixed White-Black Caribbean backgrounds with AP enrolment had a youth justice contact, the majority of whom had recorded mental health needs. Conclusion. Heightened need and intersectional inequalities among pupils enrolled in AP highlight the importance of a co-ordinated public health approach to understanding and responding to children's needs.

papers.title: Impact of transnational gentrification on the health of adults from the EPIPorto cohort: a quasi-experimental study
papers.abstract: Gentrification is a global, accelerating urban process involving complex socio-spatial transformations. Although increasingly recognised as a determinant of urban health, quantitative evidence on its population health impacts remains scarce and inconsistent, limiting evidence-informed urban policymaking, especially in rapidly gentrifying contexts. Thus, we assessed the health impact of neighbourhood-level gentrification among adults in Porto (Northern Portugal), a hotspot of transnational gentrification. A quasi-experimental study was conducted using data from the EPIPorto population-based cohort (1999-2022), with 2,485 participants at baseline. A validated, context-sensitive 16-variable index of transnational gentrification, derived from 2011 and 2021 census and tourism-accommodation data through Principal Component Analysis, enabled neighbourhood classification as gentrifying or non-gentrifying. Difference-in-differences models estimated the effect of living in gentrifying neighbourhoods on ten cardiometabolic and behavioural outcomes. Inverse probability of censoring weighting was used to account for loss to follow-up and missing data. At baseline, 26.2% of participants resided in gentrifying neighbourhoods. Residence in a gentrifying neighbourhood was associated with a statistically significant reduction in nightly sleep duration (-0.346 h; 95% CI -0.650, -0.042), with statistically significant reductions in the lower-education and [≥]65-year subgroups. No significant effects were observed for body mass index, overweight/obesity, total/HDL/LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, and tobacco or alcohol use. Transnational gentrification in Porto showed limited effects on most cardiometabolic outcomes but was associated with reduced sleep duration, suggesting that the health impacts of gentrification may initially emerge through psychosocial pathways before translating into measurable cardiometabolic changes.

papers.title: Adapting a Shared Digital Communication Intervention for Caregivers of Children with Physical Disabilities and Professionals through Co-design: A Workshop Study
papers.abstract: Introduction Caregivers of children with disabilities act as intermediaries between professionals due to fragmented communication and information sharing across sectors. The use of shared digital communication may support integrated care. Therefore, this study explored challenges and needs among caregivers and professionals and how an existing shared digital communication intervention could be adapted to support communication and coordination in this context. Methods Three future workshops involved 26 co-designers: caregivers (n=8), professionals across sectors (n=14), and software developers (n=4). Caregiver and professional data were analysed thematically, followed by matrix analysis to identify convergences, tensions, and design principles. In workshop with software developers, design principles were translated into design specifications. Results Both caregivers and professionals described how caregivers become de facto care coordinators. Clear responsibilities, continuity, and shared knowledge were identified as essential for improving communication and coordination. Shared digital communication was considered promising, but tensions emerged between accessibility and workload, and between transparency and confidentiality. The adapted intervention incorporated structured communication, shared responsibility, relational continuity, a shared overview, and a human digital coordination function. Discussion/conclusion The adapted intervention provides a foundation for cross-sector communication between caregivers and professionals and adds to the evidence base of communication solutions that may strengthen integrated care.

papers.title: Mental Health-related School Provision and Hospital Contacts among Pupils enrolled in Alternative Provision
papers.abstract: BackgroundPupils enrolled in Alternative Provision (AP) represent a highly vulnerable population, with heightened mental health need at risk of long-term educational disengagement. Examining AP enrolment in relation to mental health-related school support and hospital contacts may inform early intervention and prevention approaches to address unmet mental health need. MethodsWe analysed population-level linked school and hospital administrative data for 1.7m pupils (born 2000-2002) who attended state schools in England. We examined differences by racial-ethnic group and gender in rates and timing of AP enrolment and recording patterns of mental health-related provision and hospital contacts among pupils with AP enrolment. ResultsA majority (62.4%) of pupils with AP enrolment had recorded mental health need, highest among Mixed White-Black Caribbean pupils (74.0%). Among those in AP, 52.0% of girls with a mental health-related hospital contact had school provision, compared to 67.3% boys. For some racial-ethnic groups, schools appeared less likely to record need evident in hospital records; 17.5% boys and 36.2% girls from Mixed White-Asian backgrounds enrolled in AP had mental health-related hospital contact without school provision. ConclusionAmong pupils enrolled in AP, documented mental health need is high but unevenly recorded across systems, with inequalities by racial-ethnic group and gender.

papers.title: Stakeholder perspectives and preferences for long-acting injectables for tuberculosis treatment and prevention: a multi-regional mixed-methods study
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. MethodsWe conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. FindingsAmong 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. In Survey B, interest varied according to lived TB experience, with FGDs suggesting that previous negative experiences with injectables may have contributed to this variation. ConclusionInterest in LAIs for TB treatment and prevention was high, but lower among participants with lived TB experience. Product development and implementation should address concerns about injectables and side effects while preserving patient choice and agency.

papers.title: Acceptability and feasibility of measles vaccination, small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplementation, and their co-delivery among children aged 6-23 months in northern Nigeria: a qualitative study
papers.abstract: BackgroundUndernutrition and infectious diseases form a vicious cycle that endangers child survival in low-resource settings, including in Northern Nigeria. The NutriVax-Measles trial was designed to evaluate a strategy combining preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) distributions with community mobilization and routine immunization services for children aged 6-23 months to improve measles vaccination uptake. To inform future programs co-delivering nutrition supplementation and immunization services at scale, we aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of measles vaccination, SQ-LNS distribution, and the NutriVax strategy. MethodsA qualitative study was conducted at the end of the trial using in-depth interviews (n=53) and focus group discussions (n=8) with key stakeholders: caregivers, health care workers, community health workers, and community representatives. Thematic analysis was guided by multiple conceptual frameworks. ResultsThe majority of the participants expressed satisfaction with measles vaccines in both arms, and with SQ-LNS in the NutriVax arm, as they perceived the benefits for their childrens health. In both arms, community awareness sessions and previous experience of outbreaks were key to motivating caregivers to bring their children to healthcare centres. Although distance to health facilities was identified as one of the main barriers to accessing care, SQ-LNS was perceived as an important source of motivation to bring their child to the clinic where they subsequently received vaccination. All stakeholder groups emphasized the importance of community leaders support and targeted male sensitization to address the prevailing sociocultural norms. Additionally, improved service organization to reduce waiting time was considered crucial to enhance caregivers acceptability of the intervention. ConclusionBoth measles vaccination and SQ-LNS provision were acceptable and feasible, supporting the NutriVax strategy within primary healthcare settings in fragile health systems. Successful implementation depends on sustained community sensitization, continued engagement of fathers and community leaders, and service delivery decentralized as close as possible to beneficiaries. KEY MESSAGESO_ST_ABSWhat is already known?C_ST_ABSO_LICo-delivering small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) with routine immunization is an effective strategy to improve vaccination coverage in Northern Nigeria. Yet, evidence on how vaccination and SQ-LNS are perceived, implemented, and experienced by stakeholders at health-care and community levels remains scarce. C_LI What are the new findings?O_LISQ-LNS was an important source of motivation for caregivers to bring their children to health facilities, creating opportunities for vaccination. C_LIO_LIPersistent barriers to vaccination included socio-cultural misconceptions, gender norms, long waiting time and distance to health facilities. C_LI What do the new findings imply?O_LISustained community engagement, including targeted male sensitization, is important to improve measles vaccination acceptability. C_LIO_LISuccessful implementation of co-delivery programs also requires well-organized service delivery, with services decentralized to health facilities as close as possible to beneficiaries, particularly to reduce travel distances and waiting times. C_LI

papers.title: Investigating Climate-Driven Disruption of Malaria Transmission Following the 2022 Sindh, Pakistan Floods: An Interrupted Time Series Study
papers.abstract: Malaria remains a major global public health challenge in developing countries, with climate change intensifying its impact, particularly in vulnerable populations. Rising temperatures can expand the geographic range and local abundance of malaria vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm climates, with 25{degrees}C representing the optimal temperature for malaria transmission. In Pakistan, malaria is primarily spread through P. falciparum and P. vivax. Pakistan is one of the seven countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region that accounts for 98% of the total malaria burden in the region. Recently, after catastrophic flooding in Pakistan in 2022 and the subsequent increase in malaria incidence, it has become imperative to estimate the climate change-attributed increase in the risk of malaria. In this study, we analyze the time series malaria case incidence data from the province of Sindh, Pakistan, and the climate data to quantify climate-attributed malaria cases in Sindh, Pakistan. We fit a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to monthly case counts with interrupted time series and seasonality terms. The majority of malaria-confirmed infections were Plasmodium Vivax (40-95%) between 2016-2024, followed by Plasmodium falciparum infections. The positivity rate for malaria remained <10% until June 2022, and increased massively after the July 2022 flooding. After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that post-flooding malaria surveillance and response in flood-affected settings should anticipate not only an acute environmentally-driven surge in cases but also a subsequent period of elevated, self-sustaining transmission that may persist well beyond the resolution of the initiating environmental disruption, in this case the flooding.

papers.title: Determinants of Prehospital Management of Superficial Burns in Pediatric Patients at Health Facilities in Mazabuka District: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundBurn injuries in children are common in low-resource settings, yet little is known about how they are managed before reaching health facilities in Zambia. Early care at home plays a key role in recovery, but harmful practices are still widely used. We examined how caregivers manage superficial burns in children and identified factors linked to good prehospital care in Mazabuka District. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study between September and December 2025 among 337 caregivers of children aged 0-15 years presenting with superficial burns. The study was conducted at three health facilities in Mazabuka District. Data were collected using structured interviews and clinical records. Prehospital burn care was classified as good or poor based on the recommended first-aid practices. Associations were assessed using Firth penalised logistic regression, and results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). ResultsOnly 13.1% (44/337) of caregivers provided good prehospital burn care. Urban residence was associated with lower odds of good management (AOR 0.22; 95% CI: 0.05-0.92; p=0.038). Older caregiver age reduced the odds of good care (AOR 0.92; 95% CI: 0.86-0.98; p=0.011), while increasing child age improved it (AOR 1.25; 95% CI: 1.10-1.43; p<0.001). Longer time to reach a facility was also associated with poorer care (AOR 0.96; 95% CI 0.94-0.98; p<0.001). ConclusionGood prehospital burn care was uncommon. It was associated with time to the health facility, caregiver age, child age, and urban versus rural residence, rather than with proximity to a facility alone. Programmes should promote cooling with running water, avoidance of harmful home applications, and prompt care-seeking. Messages in routine child health services may reach caregivers of young children; additional approaches are needed for older caregivers and urban communities.

papers.title: SMALL AND SICK NEWBORN CARE: LEARNING FOR IMPLEMENTATION ACROSS AFRICA AND BEYOND: Supplement 2
papers.abstract: Background: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) reduces neonatal mortality and morbidity among preterm and low birthweight (LBW) infants, but implementation and quality vary across sub-Saharan African (SSA) hospitals. This study reports KMC coverage and quality of care for preterm and LBW neonates admitted to hospitals in the NEST360 Alliance (Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Nigeria) and examines the association between KMC provision and survival to discharge. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using routinely collected neonatal inpatient data from hospitals participating in the NEST360 Alliance. Newborns weighing under 2500g were eligible for KMC and included in coverage and quality analyses (January 2021-December 2024). Quality-of-care cascades quantified attrition along the KMC care pathway from eligibility to successful delivery, defining quality as the proportion of eligible neonates reaching each successive step. Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed the association between KMC and survival at discharge, including variation by illness severity and, among KMC recipients, by timing of initiation across severity and birthweight strata. Results: Of 375,238 neonatal admissions across 66 hospitals, 125,844 neonates were eligible for KMC and had KMC documentation available. Among these, 64,619 (51.3%) received KMC. All four countries showed improved coverage over the study period, with the largest absolute increases in Nigeria (27.6%) and Tanzania (27.4%). Excluding Kenya, where KMC timing data were unavailable, 92.1% of neonates started on KMC had a documented start date; of these 44,264 neonates, 12,934 (29.2%) were initiated on KMC on the first day of life. The quality cascade showed eligible neonates were lost at each step, from eligibility through to documented, timely, and sustained KMC. Among neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 39.4% of those started on KMC also received documented CPAP at some point during admission. After adjustment for patient-level factors, receiving KMC was associated with improved survival across all severity groups, with the greatest absolute benefit among the most critically ill neonates (adjusted predicted survival 7% vs 80% without and with KMC, respectively). Conclusion: KMC coverage improved substantially across NEST360-implementing hospitals between 2021 and 2024, demonstrating progress in implementation. However, important gaps remain in the quality and timeliness of KMC delivery. More investment in high-quality KMC implementation, supported by robust monitoring systems linked with quality improvement, are essential to improve outcomes for small and sick newborns across sub-Saharan Africa.

papers.title: Effect of results-based financing on selected maternal and child health indicators in Mayuge District, Uganda: a comparative interrupted time series analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundUganda continues to experience a high burden of maternal and child morbidity and mortality, partly due to suboptimal utilization and quality of reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health services. To address these challenges, the Ministry of Health of Uganda, with World Bank funding, implemented results-based financing (RBF) through the Uganda Reproductive, Maternal, and Child Health Services Improvement Project (URMCHIP) in selected districts. Although RBF has been implemented for nearly a decade, evidence on its impact on maternal and child health service indicators in Uganda remains limited. This study assessed the effect of RBF on selected maternal and child health indicators in Mayuge District, Uganda. MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed the records between July 2018 and June 2019 as the pre-intervention period, July 2019 to June 2021 as the intervention period, and July 2021 to June 2023 as the post-intervention period. We conducted multiple-group interrupted time-series analyses to compare trends in selected maternal and child health indicators between four intervention and three non-intervention health facilities. ResultsAfter the implementation of RBF, the number of births in the intervention facilities increased by 1.67 births per month (95% CI [0.19, 3.16]) as compared to the control facilities. The number of women receiving modern family planning methods in intervention facilities increased by 34.1 women per month (CI [25.8, 42.4] as compared to the control facilities. The number of children under five years seen at the outpatient department slightly decreased by -0.24 children per month (CI [-9.58, 9.10]). There was a decline in facility-based births and the number of clients receiving modern family planning methods following the discontinuation of results-based financing in the intervention health facilities. ConclusionsThere was an improvement in selected maternal and child health indicators in the intervention health facilities following the implementation of RBF, with a subsequent decline in facility-based births and the number of clients receiving modern family planning methods after RBF was discontinued. We recommend that policymakers consider allocating additional funds towards RBF to improve health service delivery.

papers.title: Multidimensional deprivation and brain health in older adults in rural northern Tanzania: a cross-sectional community-based study
papers.abstract: IntroductionDementia and late-life depression are rising rapidly in sub-Saharan Africa, yet prevention frameworks remain focused on individual behaviour. Multidimensional poverty is a plausible structural determinant of brain health but is rarely assessed. MethodsThis cross-sectional analysis of the community-based Akili Mali study assessed adults aged 60 years and older in three rural communities in Kilimanjaro, Tanzania. Outcomes were the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), IDEA cognitive screen, CERAD ten-word list, and verbal fluency. Deprivation was measured with a nine-indicator Alkire-Foster Multidimensional Deprivation Index. Missing data were multiply imputed; models adjusted for age, sex, education, community, comorbidity, and health behaviours. ResultsOf 1054 participants (mean age 70.2 years [SD 9.35]; 629 [59.7%] women), 840 (81.9%) of 1026 were multidimensionally deprived. Each unit increase in deprivation score predicted a higher GDS-15 score ({beta} 4.83, 95% CI 3.82 to 5.83), higher odds of screen-positive depression (odds ratio 17.18, 6.89 to 42.83), lower IDEA score ({beta} -1.97, -2.97 to -0.97), and lower verbal fluency ({beta} -2.57, -3.77 to -1.36; all p<0.001). CERAD measures and self-reported impairment showed no association. At community level this gradient inverted: the most deprived community had the lowest depression and highest cognition, yet perceived social standing did not differ. ConclusionMultidimensional deprivation was near-universal and independently associated with worse brain health. The community-level inversion, with perceived social standing equivalent across communities of unequal material circumstances, indicates that absolute deprivation alone does not explain the distribution of brain health. Relative position and community resilience are priorities for study. FundingMedical Research Council (MR/X03092X/1). Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSMultidimensional poverty has been linked to dementia in South Africa and to depressive symptoms in Kenya, but no study in East Africa has examined it against both cognition and depression in the same older population, and dementia prevention frameworks remain oriented to individually modifiable risk. What this study addsMultidimensional deprivation affected four in five older adults in rural Kilimanjaro and was independently associated with greater depressive symptom burden and poorer measured cognition, yet the relationship inverted between communities, with the most materially deprived community showing the lowest depression and the strongest cognitive performance while rating its social standing no lower than the least deprived. How this study might affect research, practice or policyDifferent dimensions of deprivation predict different outcomes, so anti-poverty measures intended to protect brain health may need to be dimension-specific, and the community-level inversion is a caution that deprivation data aggregated to community level can reverse the relationships operating within those communities.

papers.title: The life course shaping of quality of life in older age: does childhood poverty associate with control, autonomy, self-realisation and pleasure? A retrospective and prospective study of HRS, ELSA, SHARE and TILDA cohorts
papers.abstract: Later-life quality of life is increasingly recognised as a life-course achievement, yet ageing research has focused more on dysfunction and decline than on positive wellbeing. This study examines whether childhood poverty shapes later-life quality of life, measured by CASP: control, autonomy, self-realisation and pleasure. METHODSI analysed harmonised data from 59,569 adults aged over 50 in 29 countries, drawn from HRS, ELSA, SHARE and TILDA (U.S. Health and Retirement Study, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing). Childhood poverty was modelled as a latent class from retrospectively reported childhood material circumstances, acknowledging recall error in such reports. Country fixed-effects linear models estimated associations with CASP, first adjusting for age, sex and country, then adding education, marital status and later-life wealth. RESULTSOne in five participants grew up in poverty (22.9%). Mean CASP was 38 out of 48. Initially childhood poverty was associated with a 1.2-point lower CASP score; after complete adjustment the penalty attenuated but remained durable at 0.7 points. Education, partnership and wealth were independently associated with higher wellbeing but did not erase the penalty. Predicted age profiles showed poverty penalty in every country. They also revealed striking national differences: Nordic countries achieved markedly higher CASP levels than several Eastern European countries; Finns aged 90 had similar levels of positive wellbeing to Latvians two decades younger. CONCLUSIONChildhood poverty leaves a durable mark on later-life positive wellbeing, while welfare contexts appear to lift overall CASP levels. Reducing child poverty and strengthening social protection are therefore lifelong wellbeing policies.

papers.title: Wastewater pathogen composition in Atlanta, GA prior to and during the 2026 FIFA World Cup
papers.abstract: Mass gatherings can have many impacts on public health, including facilitating the spread of infectious diseases. Alternative surveillance modalities, such as wastewater-based surveillance (WBS), can complement traditional clinical surveillance. We utilized WBS to examine the influence of the 2026 FIFA World Cup (FWC26) on the range of infectious pathogens in Atlanta, GA surrounding matches held in the city. Samples (n = 102) were collected from three water reclamation facilities between April and July of 2026 (34 collection days) and tested using the BIOFIRE(R) WATCHFIRE Respiratory (19 targets) and Gastrointestinal (22 targets) PCR Pathogen Panels. Primary data analysis included a temporal comparison of wastewater pathogen profiles before (April 1 to June 10; n = 60) and during (June 15 to July 15; n = 30) the FWC26 across the three facilities using a modified Poisson model with Bonferroni correction. There were no statistically significant differences in target detection between the two periods. Samples collected after the FWC26 (July 20 to 29; n = 12) were included in a sensitivity analysis which showed a statistically significant increase in SARS-CoV-2 (RR = 3.21, 95% CI = 1.40-7.39; p = 0.01, p-adjusted = 0.048) during and after the tournament compared to before. However, this coincided with regional and national increases in SARS-CoV-2 detection in wastewater, suggesting ongoing community burden. Wide confidence intervals, lack of quantitative data, and limited data collection after the matches limit our conclusions. This study demonstrates the use of qualitative, multiplexed PCR assays for WBS during a mass gathering sporting event. ImportanceMass gatherings can have numerous public health implications, including facilitating the spread of infectious diseases. Surveillance, both with clinical tracking of cases and through alternative methods, such as wastewater-based surveillance, can inform bio-preparedness efforts. Our study demonstrates the use of qualitative PCR assays to capture population-level pathogen information surrounding the 2026 FIFA World Cup matches held in Atlanta, GA.

papers.title: Epidemiology of acute respiratory infections in adult patients in Hospices Civils de Lyon, France, between October 2016 and April 2025
papers.abstract: BackgroundMultiple viruses can cause acute respiratory infections (ARI), impacting morbidity, mortality and hospital resources. The objective of this study was to describe viral circulation among patients with ARI, patients characteristics and severity outcomes. MethodsA retrospective cohort was assembled using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France. Adult patients ([≥]18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection were included. Administrative variables and laboratory results collected during the stay were extracted. Results103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients were included. The number of eligible stays increased substantially since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing. Following disruption during the pandemic, winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza and RSV detections re-emerged after 2022. Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged [≥]80 years. Patients aged [≥]65 years had longer hospitalisations (median 10 vs 8 days, p<0.001), twice in-hospital mortality rate (14% vs 7%, p<0.001), less frequent ICU admission (21% vs 33%, p<0.001) and use of respiratory support than younger adults. Influenza was the virus associated with the shortest length of stays, hMPV was associated with the longest in younger adults. ConclusionsReal-world hospital data are valuable for surveillance of viral circulation, early identification of patients at risk of deterioration, and may be used to evaluate the impact of preventive intervention in community.

papers.title: Estimated impacts of mandatory sodium reformulation targets on sodium consumption, health outcomes, health sector costs and health equity in Aotearoa New Zealand
papers.abstract: AimsCardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), including for M[a]ori, the Indigenous population. Sodium intake is a modifiable CVD risk factor. In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) released sodium reduction benchmarks for 58 packaged food categories. We aimed to estimate the health, health-sector cost, and equity impacts of mandating these benchmarks in NZ. MethodsNationally representative data on household food purchases, packaged food sodium content, and dietary intake were used to estimate baseline sodium consumption (2011) and changes following implementation of the WHO benchmarks. A dietary multi-state life-table model estimated impacts on health-adjusted life years (HALYs) and health system costs (2011 NZ$, 3% discount rate) over the remaining lifetime of the 2011 NZ population (n = 4.4 million). Analyses examined impacts by sex and for M[a]ori. ResultsMandatory reformulation was estimated to reduce sodium intake by 470 mg/day per person (1.18 g salt), a 22% reduction from baseline. Across population groups, age-standardised reductions ranged from 380 to 660 mg/day (22-23%), generating an estimated 55,600 HALYs (95% uncertainty interval 19,100-90,000) and NZ$535.2 million in health-system cost savings (95% UI: 183.0-914.6 million) over the population lifetime. M[a]ori gained 11,600 HALYs (95% UI: 4,900-17,700), equivalent to 17.2 HALYs per 1,000 population, compared with 11.8 per 1,000 among non-M[a]ori. ConclusionMandating WHO sodium benchmarks in NZ could substantially reduce sodium intake, improve population health, reduce health sector costs, and advance health equity. Findings support adoption of this strategy in Aotearoa NZ. Lay summaryRequiring food manufacturers in Aotearoa New Zealand to meet World Health Organization sodium (salt) targets could reduce salt intake, prevent disease, save health sector costs, and improve health equity for M[a]ori. O_LIMandatory sodium reformulation of packaged foods was estimated to reduce average sodium intake by 470 mg per person per day (equivalent to 1.18 g of salt), a 22% reduction from current levels, resulting in health benefits across the population. C_LIO_LIThe policy was estimated to generate 55,600 health-adjusted life years and save NZ$535 million in healthcare costs over the populations lifetime, with greater health gains per person for M[a]ori than non-M[a]ori, helping reduce health inequities. C_LI

papers.title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
papers.abstract: IntroductionBetween 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHOs 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. MethodsI analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. ResultsWomen held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). ConclusionsBefore the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSMarburg virus research has been mapped by output, country and keyword, and the United States dominates it. In infectious-disease and COVID-19 research, women and researchers from African countries are under-represented in senior author positions. What this study addsTo my knowledge, this is the first study of who leads Marburg virus research. Before the 2023-2025 outbreaks, women held one in five last-author positions, only one in four papers about an African country had a first author from that country, and 69% of funded papers acknowledged a US funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity were each covered by fewer than 8% of papers. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThe findings give a baseline to track whether recent African-led outbreak responses change who leads the field. Funders can direct support to institutions in affected countries and to neglected WHO priorities, and journals can expect local leadership of research done in those countries.
